## TL;DR

Git worker children were never closed in tests and had no production cap. `getGitWorker(root)` keeps one worker per repository root for the life of the process, and each worker starts two Bun children (a bulk lane and a fast lane). Nothing in the test suite closed them, so every test file that drove server code against a temp root left its children running until the vitest fork exited. In a broader scoped run I reproduced the leak: the process count peaked at 153 `git-worker-entry` processes, all parented by live vitest forks.

The fix does three things. Test files close every git worker in their per-file `afterAll`. Production caps live git worker children at four per process: starting a child over the cap first stops the least-recently-used idle child, and that lane respawns on its next request. A new test asserts that no child survives teardown and that the cap holds across many repositories. The scoped check on the changed git-worker suites passes (8 files, 73 tests).

## Work and rationale

I started from the task's suspicion that a pool was never closed. Reading `src/server/git-worker.ts` confirmed it: the `workers` map is module state keyed by root, `getGitWorker` never evicts, and `closeGitWorker` is the only path that kills a child. A grep showed production code calls `getGitWorker(config.root)` from many server modules (handoff, done, shot capture, integration orchestrator, review), so any test that reaches those paths with a temp root creates a worker. Only three test files call `closeGitWorker`.

Vitest's forks pool reuses processes across files, but module state is per file. Each file's workers become unreachable when the file ends, and the child keeps running because the parent never sends a close. The child exits only on stdin EOF, which happens when its fork exits, so the leak lasts for the whole run.

The change, in order:

1. **Teardown.** `closeAllGitWorkers()` closes every registered worker and any live lane. `process-guard.ts` already runs a per-file `afterAll` for spawned helpers; I added the git worker close there. It uses a dynamic import so files that never touch git don't load the module. I checked that no test mocks `git-worker.js`, because a mock without the new export would break the teardown.

2. **Production cap.** I added a module-level set of lanes that own a live child, and `MAX_GIT_WORKER_CHILDREN = 4`. `ensureChild` refreshes recency when reusing a child and, before spawning a new one, stops the least-recently-used idle lane's child. I chose to stop the child rather than close the lane. A closed worker rejects every later call, and several callers hold a worker reference across `await`s (for example `review-tree-identity.ts`), so closing would turn an eviction into a failure. A stopped child only costs a respawn. Busy lanes are never stopped, so a burst of in-flight requests can exceed the cap until they finish. The doc comment and `docs/server-git-worker.md` say so.

3. **Tests.** `src/ui-app/tests/git-worker-process-cap.test.ts` counts real children by parent pid (`ps -axo pid,ppid,stat,command`), so other sessions' workers don't affect the result, and ignores zombies. The first test starts a child, calls `closeAllGitWorkers()`, and polls until none remain. The second opens `MAX_GIT_WORKER_CHILDREN * 2` repositories in sequence, checks `gitWorkerChildCount()` after each, and confirms an evicted repository still answers. I used the internal lane count for the cap assertion because a SIGKILLed child can still appear in `ps` for a moment, which would make a process-count assertion flaky.

## Approaches tried

- **Closing each worker in its own test file.** Rejected: it would need every caller to remember it, and it doesn't bound production. The three files that already do this showed the pattern is easy to miss.
- **Closing a worker on eviction.** Rejected for the reason above: it breaks callers that hold the worker across awaits.
- **Counting processes instead of lanes for the cap.** The lane count is exact and immediate. Process counts lag because SIGKILL delivery is asynchronous, so I kept process counts only for the teardown check, where a poll is appropriate.
- **Static import of the worker module in `process-guard.ts`.** Works, but loads the module in every test file. The dynamic import keeps the cost off files that never use git.

## Challenges and blockers

- **Reproduction noise.** Other RepoOS sessions and the main checkout's server run `git-worker-entry` on this machine, so a raw process count is meaningless. My measurements filter by parent pid or subtract the baseline of about 3–5 processes that were already running.
- **My own stale runs.** My first two background attempts to reproduce were cut off when the shell call returned, and one vitest tree kept running. I found the two `run-tests` roots and their descendants and terminated those PIDs. That removed 148 processes from my own runs. I didn't touch any other session's processes.
- **Peak after the fix is not an exact bound.** The sampled peak in the post-fix run was 10 processes across the machine. Other sessions were running, so that number doesn't prove the cap; the lane-count test is the real check.
- **Full scoped check did not finish locally.** `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check` died twice mid-suite (at 312/821 and then at 298/821 tests) with no failure message and no exit line. The first death was on a shell restart; the second came about 23 minutes into the run. The logs show no failing test. The changed git-worker suites pass (8 files, 73 tests). The full gate has not run to completion here, so RepoOS's server-side check is the first full run of this change.
- **Sampling tool behaviour.** Background subshells inside a foreground call were terminated when the call returned. I moved the sampler and vitest into one background script, which kept the sampler alive for the whole run.

## Key learnings

- A process-wide registry that owns OS processes needs an explicit teardown and a bound, even when production only ever has one key. Tests exercise many keys in one process, which production never does.
- Evicting a resource that callers hold by reference should stop the resource and keep the handle usable, not invalidate the handle.
- Count what your code owns (lanes with live children) when you assert a bound. Asserting on OS process listings is a slower, racier signal.
- The cap value of four is a judgement: one repository needs two processes, so the cap leaves room for one more repository before eviction starts. If the production server ever serves several repositories at once, this value is the first thing to revisit.
